activity: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
story:
The automatic doors of the pharmacy exhaled warm air over Robert's shoes, and he stood for a moment in the fluorescent hush of the vitamin aisle, rehearsing. On Monday he would stand in front of Ms. Rodríguez's peer health class and explain consent, contraception, and where to get tested, because Ms. Rodríguez had said he was good at explaining things, which he suspected was a polite way of saying she was tired. He had a basket. In the basket were a box of condoms, a sheet of clinic appointment slips he'd picked up from the campus health office, and a bottle of vitamins that was only there so his hands would have something to hold.

He walked the aisles slowly, building the lesson in his head. Consent first, because it came first: a yes that could be taken back, a yes that couldn't be bought with dinner or a month of texting. Then contraception, which was ancillary to consent but not to consequence, the practical arithmetic that followed from a decision already made. He turned these sentences over the way he turned a proof in math, checking each one for a soft spot. Somewhere behind him a cart wheel squeaked and stopped.

"You're doing the thing," said a voice. "The talking-to-yourself thing." It was Anastasia, in the green staff vest, restocking cough syrup two shelves away. She'd been in his chemistry class since sophomore year and had watched him mutter through every exam. She nodded at the basket. "You rob somebody?"

"Peer health presentation. Ms. Rodríguez volunteered me."

"Condoms, appointment slips, and vitamin D," she said. "That's either a lesson plan or a very boring weekend." She came around the shelf and leaned on the shelf edge. "You know where you're sending people? The clinic on Marsh Street?"

He did. He'd walked past it twice to time the route from school, feeling a strange rectitude about knowing the hours, the sliding glass doors, the tray of pamphlets by the front desk. He told her this, and she laughed, but not unkindly, and asked what he'd say if someone said they felt fine and didn't need a test.

The question caught him. He had a card in his back pocket, notes he'd written at his desk at midnight, and he took it out and looked for the line. He found it, read it once, and put it away, because reading it aloud felt like reciting, not explaining. "I'd say feeling fine doesn't prove anything," he said slowly. "Chlamydia and gonorrhea often cause no symptoms, so testing is the only reliable way for a person to know whether they have one." Anastasia nodded, said "okay," and moved off toward the registers, and Robert stood in the aisle feeling the sentence settle into him, less like a fact he'd memorized than a door he'd finally walked through.

From two aisles over, Caden watched the whole thing without meaning to. He'd come in for his mother's antacid and had stopped at the endcap of razors when he heard Robert's voice doing its careful, level explaining, and something in him had gone still. Three weeks ago, at Peter's party, there had been a girl whose name he was ashamed he half remembered, and they had been careful, mostly careful, and he felt fine. He had been telling himself that for twenty days. He felt fine, therefore he was fine; the logic had the shape of airtight and the substance of fog. Now Robert's sentence was in his head, rearranging it. No symptoms. Only reliable way to know. He picked up the antacid and walked toward the registers with his eyes on the floor.

At the register Anastasia rang him up, and he almost said something twice. The second time, what came out was, "That clinic. Marsh Street. Do they take walk-ins?" She said until four on weekdays. He paid, took the bag, and then stood there a moment with his hand on the strap of it. Robert was coming up the aisle with his basket, still mouthing pieces of his talk, and Caden understood that Robert would never know, that the presentation would happen Monday to a room of half-listening kids and it would matter to exactly one of them for reasons Robert couldn't imagine, and that this was fine, that maybe this was how good things worked, obliquely, without receipts.

"Hey," Caden said, when Robert reached the front. "Good luck Monday. You'll be good at it."

Robert looked at him a second too long, some instinct flickering and going out. "Thanks," he said, and set his basket on the counter. Behind the window, the afternoon had gone gray, and the sign at the Marsh Street clinic, though neither of them could see it from here, had just been switched, by a nurse with cold hands, to read Open.

story:
The tuner app on Leighton's phone showed the number like a verdict: 440. Ms. Korhonen raised her oboe, gave a long, steady note, and the community band in the school auditorium answered her in a wash of sound that Jesse could feel in his teeth. He blew into his clarinet and watched the needle on his own phone drift flat, so he pushed the barrel in a millimetre, then another, until the needle settled and the words A above middle C glowed steady at the top of the screen. Beside him, Franco was already there, swaying slightly, eyes closed, as though tuning were something you could feel rather than measure.

Jesse had started clarinet in September, three years behind everyone else in the band, and the autumn had been a long education in how much he didn't know. He knew now that the whole ensemble tuned to a single note, and that the number 440 meant hertz, vibrations per second, and that it hadn't just happened; the International Organization for Standardization had formalized it, and someone at rehearsal, probably Leighton, had mentioned offhandedly that it was called ISO 16. Leighton knew things like that the way other people knew sports scores. "It's literally an international standard," Leighton had said, as if that settled something, and maybe it did.

The problem was that Franco tuned by ear and openly scorned the app. "Machines don't hear the room," Franco said that Tuesday, snapping his case shut while the flute section fluttered through their scales. He gestured at the auditorium's high ceiling, the folding chairs, the curtain half-lifted over the stage like a held breath. "This place swallows certain frequencies. You tune to the room, not to a number." Franco had been playing since he was seven. Franco had a solo in the December concert. Jesse had a third-clarinet part with forty-two rests in it.

He tried it Franco's way that week. He closed his eyes and listened to Ms. Korhonen's oboe, tried to dissolve the boundary between her sound and his, and sometimes, for a second, the two notes locked together and the auditorium seemed to hum from somewhere subterranean, a warmth rising through the soles of his shoes. Then a trumpet behind him went sharp, or a chair scraped, and the feeling dissolved. The app, meanwhile, sat in his pocket like a small honest witness. He began to understand that he was caught between two loyalties: Leighton's faith in the standard, the clean number agreed on by an international body, and Franco's older, messier claim that music was a thing done by ears in rooms. The band, he noticed, didn't argue about it. The adults had achieved a kind of detente: the oboe gave the note, everyone tuned to the oboe, and nobody asked what the oboe was tuned to.

The night before the December concert, Ms. Korhonen kept the clarinet section after rehearsal. "Jesse, play your line from letter C," she said, and he did, the slow rising phrase he'd been practising in his bedroom with the door shut. When he finished she was quiet a moment, and the silence was worse than criticism. "You're playing all the notes," she said finally. "You're playing none of the music." She had him play it again while she listened with her eyes closed, and afterward she said only, "You're counting, not breathing. Try breathing."

That night he sat on his bed with the tuner app open, the needle floating at rest, and thought about what each of them valorized: Leighton the standard, Franco the room, Ms. Korhonen something harder to name that lived in neither. He decided, without quite being able to say why, that the number and the ear weren't enemies, that 440 was a door rather than a destination, a place everyone agreed to stand so that they could hear each other. But he could hear Franco's voice arguing back, and honestly he wasn't sure the debate was settled, only that he'd chosen a side for now.

At the concert, the auditorium filled with winter coats and program rustle. Before the downbeat, Ms. Korhonen lifted her oboe and gave the A, and Jesse watched Franco, who had left his phone in his case across the room, lean toward the sound with his whole body. Jesse leaned in too. He let the note fill his mouth, checked his barrel against it by feel, and when the needle in his pocket, had he looked, would have shown 440, he closed his eyes and stopped looking.

The slow phrase at letter C came and went. He breathed through it, and something locked, briefly, and then the trumpets swelled and carried everything forward. Afterward, in the crowded aisle, Franco clapped him on the shoulder, hard, and Leighton held up his phone with the tuner app open, the number still glowing. "Four forty," Leighton said, grinning. "You were dead on."

story:
The grocery store on Milner Road was almost empty by eight, the freezers humming their one long note, and Amy stood at the meat counter holding her mother's list like scripture. Her mother had gone to bed with a fever, and her father was working the night shift, which left the Sunday roast to Amy, who had never cooked one. The list said, in her mother's slanted hand, "top round, 3 lb, nothing fancy," and beneath that, "oven 325, pull at 130, medium-rare." She had watched her mother do it a hundred times without ever once paying attention.

"Take the one at the back," said the butcher, reaching without being asked. "The ones up front have been sitting under the light all day."

At the till, Ms. Mensah from two doors down was buying ginger and lemons, and she looked at the pink slab in Amy's basket and then at Amy's face. "Your mother's unwell," she said. It wasn't a question. "Do you have a thermometer? An instant-read one, not the kind that stays in the oven."

"We have one," Amy said. "I think." She wasn't sure where her mother kept it, and she was too tired to pretend otherwise. Ms. Mensah pressed a lemon into her bag as well, for tea, and left before Amy could thank her properly.

The oven dial felt anachronistic in her hands, stiff and unlabeled, older than anything else in the kitchen, and she turned it to 325 by counting the clicks. She found the thermometer in the drawer with the broken rubber bands and the takeout menus, wiped it off, and texted Samia a photograph of the roast with the caption, "My mother's sick and I have to make this and I'm terrified." While the meat seared in the pan, filling the kitchen with a smell that made the whole thing seem suddenly possible, Samia's reply came in three bubbles. The first said, "You've got this." The second said, "My uncle is a chef and he says the number on the thermometer isn't the finish line." The third said, "He calls it carryover cooking. The roast keeps cooking after it comes out. A big one can go up several degrees just sitting there resting."

Amy read the messages twice, leaning against the counter with the spatula still in her hand. Her mother's note said pull at 130, and her mother's roasts were always medium-rare, always pink and quiet in the center. If Samia's uncle was right, then the note wasn't wrong so much as incomplete, written for hands that already knew what the note left out. There was a strange comfort in that: instructions as a conversation between people who trusted each other's silence. There was also a problem. Several degrees past 130 was past medium-rare, and she had no way to know how many degrees several meant.

She decided to split the difference, since that was all she could do, and she set the thermometer's alarm five degrees below the target. When it chirped at 125, she pulled the roast out, tented it with foil the way she had seen her mother do, and stood over it wanting to beseech it, almost, to stop. It sat there steaming under its silver hood like something with its own physiology, its own warm internal weather, doing whatever it was doing regardless of her. Sonia called while it rested, and Amy told her about the fever, the butcher, the messages from Samia, and the five degrees she had gambled on. "So you don't actually know," Sonia said. "No," Amy said. "I don't."

When she carved it, ten minutes later, the center came out rose-pink fading to grey at the edges, a little more done than her mother's, a little less than ruined. She set three plates, carried one to her mother's room on a tray, and sat on the edge of the bed while her mother propped herself up and ate two slices, slowly, with the fever still in her eyes. "It's good," her mother said. "It's a touch past where I make it." Amy nodded and looked at the tray. "Next time I'll pull it earlier," she said. "Next time," her mother said, and reached for the salt.

activity: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
story:
The cultural festival had taken over the park with the cheerful chaos of a yard sale and a passport office combined, and Zoey was standing under a banner that read INTERFAITH DIALOGUE TENT, ALL WELCOME, holding a paper plate of dumplings she was too nervous to eat. In twenty minutes she was supposed to argue, in front of strangers, whether an ancient religious rule about not charging interest still applied to modern life. She had drawn the side arguing that it did not, which was unfortunate, because the more she read, the less sure she became.

"You look like someone defamed your dumplings," said Ashlyn, appearing beside her with two cups of mango juice. "Or do I mean maligned? Chew. Swallow. Then tell me."

"You can't defame dumplings, they have no reputation to ruin." Zoey took a bite anyway. "I'm supposed to use the text itself. Ms. Popescu said no opinions until the words are on the table. The trouble is the words are three thousand years old and I keep finding exactly what I already think in them."

Ashlyn handed her the juice. "That sounds like a you problem."

They found Benedict inside the tent, already seated at a folding table laid with photocopied passages, looking smug in the specific way of someone who has practiced. He was arguing the rule still applied. Ms. Popescu, who had organized the tent and knew six languages and once, reportedly, corrected a rabbi's Hebrew at a bus stop, sat at the side with a thermos and no expression at all.

The tent smelled of incense from the next booth over and hot sugar from the churro cart. Someone's toddler was conducting an aggressive negotiation with a balloon. Benedict opened by reading the verse aloud, the one forbidding usury among one's own people, and then said, in his debate-club voice, "The principle is clear. Exploiting the poor through loans is wrong in every century."

"Wait," Zoey said. Her heart was going like the drum circle two booths down. "Say the last part again. 'That the poor may live with you.' The rule is about a village where the poor person is your neighbor, where you'd see them every day at the well. That's not a bank. That's not a mortgage at five percent over thirty years."

"So context excuses everything?"

"No. Context is the whole thing." She hadn't planned to say that. "Ms. Popescu told me a word last week and I wrote it on my hand." She turned her palm over, where EXEGESIS was smudged half illegible beside a dumpling grease stain. "Exegesis means drawing the meaning out of the text, from its own words and its own context. The opposite is eisegesis, reading your ideas into it. I think I've been doing the second one all week. I found a verse that agreed with me and acted like the verse wrote itself for my side."

Benedict blinked. "You're undermining your own case. In public. This is the worst strategy I have ever witnessed."

"I'm not undermining it, I'm testing it." She pulled out the photocopy, its margins crowded with her handwriting. "Look. If I take the words in their setting, the rule protects specific poor neighbors from specific lenders who could ruin them by spring. A modern credit union making a small loan to help someone buy a work van isn't that. But," and here she slowed down, because this was the part she had only worked out on the bus that morning, "payday lenders charging desperate people ruinous rates is exactly that. Same power, same desperation, same ruined spring. So maybe the rule applies and doesn't, depending on which modern thing you hold it up against."

"That's fence-sitting," Benedict said, but with less conviction than before. He looked at his own notes. He looked, Zoey noticed, at his notes for a long time. "I did the other thing, didn't I. The eisegesis thing. My uncle got crushed by debt and I found every verse that condemned lenders and quoted those and skipped the parts about forgiving debts every seventh year, which is way more radical than anything I was proposing."

"Maybe we both did," Zoey said. "Maybe everybody does first and notices later."

"Notice," said Ms. Popescu from the side, holding up her thermos as if toasting them, "is the whole assignment." She poured coffee, offered the tent a rare smile, and added nothing else, which was apparently her way of saying the debate could continue without adult supervision.

A woman from the audience, wearing a sari and a lanyard that said FESTIVAL VOLUNTEER, raised her hand. "So which side wins?"

"That depends," Benedict said, "on whether you want the text's answer or ours, and I no longer trust us to tell the difference." He said it cheerfully, the way he said everything, but he folded his notes in half as he said it, and Zoey thought the fold looked somehow permanent.

Outside the tent the drum circle had reached the part where toddlers lose their minds with joy. Zoey found she had finished her mango juice at some point without noticing, and that Ashlyn had quietly eaten the rest of her dumplings.

"You owe me a churro," Zoey said.

"For what?"

"For the margin notes on my hand. I'm keeping them. I'll need them in college, when somebody's wrong on the internet at me."

Ashlyn stood, brushed sugar off her jeans, and held out a hand to pull Zoey up. "Come on, we'll split one. But I'm choosing the topping, because honestly, your judgment is jaundiced by that debate tent, and a churro needs subtlety."

"You've been waiting all afternoon to say that."

story:
The new classroom smelled like floor wax and someone else's history. Gabriella took the empty desk by the window because the teacher, Mr. Wang, had not yet assigned seats, and she wanted a few days of choosing before the choosing was taken away. Behind her, two students argued about whether the vending machine on the second floor had ever given anyone two bags of chips by accident. She knew their names from attendance, Devin and Cayden, but they didn't know hers yet, and the gap felt physical, like a pane of glass.

At lunch she sat alone and texted her best friend from back home, whose replies were getting shorter in a way that neither of them had named out loud. After school, instead of taking the bus, she walked until she found the public library, a brick building with a stained ceiling and a radiator that knocked like a small animal trapped in the wall. She chose a table near the periodicals and did her homework there, and when the radiator knocked she felt almost at home, which was a sentence she hated herself for forming.

She went back the next afternoon, and the one after that. On the fourth day, Devin sat down across from her with a chemistry binder and no explanation. He did his work. She did hers. When he left he said, "You're in Wang's third period, right? He does a seating chart by Friday, so enjoy the window while it lasts." She laughed before she could decide whether to.

Cayden appeared the following week, drawn in by Devin, and it turned out Cayden's mother worked at the library and Cayden had been coming there since childhood with a satchel of rubber-banded cards from the old paper catalogue. "This is basically my living room," Cayden said, spreading out flashcards on the table Gabriella had come to think of as hers. She bristled and then didn't, because the bristling required a claim she wasn't sure she had earned. A table couldn't be possessed by sitting at it for nine days. Or maybe it could. She left the question open and dealt the flashcards into two piles.

It was Mr. Wang who set the assignment that changed the shape of her afternoons: a research essay on a social problem, any problem, with a real scholarly source. Gabriella, who had been privately researching loneliness the way other people researched illnesses, reading about its epidemiology late at night, the studies tracking how isolation spread through populations and shortened lives, typed "loneliness public spaces" into the library database mostly out of stubbornness. She wanted her problem to be legitimate. She wanted, though she would not have admitted it in those words, to predicate her unhappiness on something structural, so that it wasn't a personal failing but a condition with a name.

The database gave her a book by a sociologist named Ray Oldenburg, published in 1989, called The Great Good Place. She read the first pages at the periodicals table with her hand flat on the cover. Oldenburg had named these places, the cafes and libraries where people met outside home and work. "Third places," she said aloud, before she could stop herself.

"Did you just quote something?" Cayden leaned over the divider between their chairs.

"It's this book. He calls them third places. Home is first, work is second, and then places like this. Like the library. Like this table, actually." She felt foolish saying it, and also lighter, as if someone had handed her a map of terrain she had been crossing blind.

"Then this table is a third place," Devin said, "which means it's public property, which means you can't glare at me when I take your chair." He took her chair anyway, the one by the radiator, and she let him, and the letting felt like something.

She wrote the essay over two weeks, mostly at that table, with Cayden correcting her citations and Devin arguing that her statistics about isolation weren't germane to a paper about physical spaces, that she was mixing up two different problems. They fought about it for a whole afternoon, low-voiced under the NO TALKING sign, and she ended up cutting half her favourite paragraphs, which hurt. But she also ended up knowing something she hadn't before: that she had been treating the move as a wound that time would close on its own, and that instead she had built something small and deliberate, a table, two people, a regular hour, and that building it had cost her the story she used to tell about herself, the girl who was only waiting to go back.

The night before the essay was due, her old best friend called, and they talked for forty minutes, and it was almost like before, except that Gabriella kept noticing the silences where the friend's new friends were apparently waiting. She said nothing about noticing. She said goodnight, and then sat on her bed with her laptop and reread the last page, where she had written that she wasn't sure yet whether a place became a third place because of what it was or because of who kept returning to it, and that she suspected the answer mattered.

On Friday, Mr. Wang posted the seating chart. Gabriella's name was in the middle of the room, far from the window. She stood in front of the list for a moment, then took out her phone and typed to Devin and Cayden: library at four, I'm claiming the radiator chair back.

activity: to explain comparative advantage and why two countries both gain from trading
story:
The porch boards at Grandfather's house had been painted so many times that the newest coat cracked along the older ones, and Adam sat on the top step with his economics textbook open on his knees, reading the same paragraph for the fourth time. Comparative advantage, said the paragraph, was why two countries could both gain from trade even when one of them was better at everything. He understood the arithmetic. He could reproduce the little table of hours-per-unit on a quiz without thinking. What he could not do was say it out loud in a way that survived contact with an actual human being, and the class debate was Monday.

"Put that book away for ten minutes," Grandfather said from the doorway, holding two glasses of lemonade. "You'll ruin your eyes, and then who'll read my mail for me?"

"You get bills, Grandpa. Nothing good."

"Bills are suspenseful. You never know which one's an ambush." He sat down in the green chair that only he was allowed to sit in, and Adam closed the book, which felt like shutting a door on a room where he'd left something burning.

Mr. Boateng came through the gap in the hedge the way he always did on Saturdays, carrying a chessboard under his arm like a briefcase. "I heard voices. Also I heard the word trade, which means either economics or gossip, and I brought the board either way." He set it up on the porch rail, and the three of them fell into the slow Saturday ritual: Grandfather's obdurate defense, Mr. Boateng's patient knights, Adam losing quickly and then losing more slowly as the afternoon wore on.

Somewhere in the second game, Adam made the mistake of feeling confident. "We're doing a debate on trade," he said. "I've got the easy side, honestly. Free trade. It's just math. Both countries end up richer, total income goes up. You'd have to be against arithmetic to argue with it."

The lemonade glass stopped halfway to Grandfather's mouth. He set it down on the rail with a small click, closer to a click than a set-down, and moved a pawn in a way that had nothing to do with chess. Mr. Boateng looked at the board and did not look up, which Adam was too pleased with himself to notice.

"Richer on paper," Grandfather said. "Whose paper?"

"The country's paper. The whole country's income." Adam heard his own voice go enthusiastic and did not hear anything underneath the silence that followed it. "My teacher says even if one country's better at everything, both still gain. They call it comparative advantage. Each one does the thing it's comparatively best at, and trade makes the total bigger. It's elegant, honestly. Economists practically lionize the guy who came up with it."

"Mm," said Grandfather.

"Grandpa worked at the Hartwell mill for thirty-one years," Mr. Boateng said, quietly, still studying the board as though the pieces had asked him not to intervene.

Adam looked up. He had heard about the mill his whole life in the abstract way you hear about a grandparent's hometown, a place, a fact of biography. What he had never once heard, and what he understood now he had somehow never asked, was how it ended. He waited, and Grandfather took his time, the way he took his time with everything except bill ambushes.

"Closed in my last year before I would've had the pension top-up," Grandfather said finally. "Cheaper cloth coming in from overseas. Same cloth, near enough. Same as ours, but cheaper, because their wages were lower and their government subsidized the plant. So the total went up somewhere, I'm sure. On somebody's paper." He moved his rook. "Eleven hundred of us in that parking lot on a Tuesday morning. You can do the arithmetic on that, too."

The textbook sat beside Adam on the step, and for a moment he wanted to open it and hide behind it, because both things were suddenly true at once and they refused to cancel out. "Both things are true," he said slowly. "That's the part I can't say in a debate. The country's total income goes up. And you still lost your job. Both. Not one or the other."

"I'm not saying trade's the devil," Grandfather said. "My television came from somewhere. My car. I'm saying when somebody tells me everybody wins, I want to know what happened to the everybody who worked in building twelve." Mr. Boateng moved a knight and said nothing, which for him was a speech.

"Check," Grandfather said, and then, almost smiling, "Check, and also, you left your queen where my grandson could learn something from watching her get taken."

Adam texted Mickael that night from the guest room, lying under the ceiling fan that clicked like a slow clock. how do you argue both sides of something without sounding like you believe nothing. Mickael wrote back immediately, which meant he was also supposed to be doing homework: you don't sound like nothing, you sound like a person who read more than one book. Elyse, added to the thread, sent a single thumbs up and then, three minutes later, a photograph of her own textbook with the corner folded and one word underlined: losers. The debate could go two ways now, and Adam honestly did not know which way he would argue until he stood up there, only that he would not argue it the way he'd argued it on the porch.

He came down the next morning to find Grandfather at the kitchen table with the economics textbook open in front of him, reading glasses low on his nose, one finger on the little table of hours-per-unit.

"You left this on the step," Grandfather said, not looking up. "Sit down. Explain it to me again, slower. And this time, don't skip the part about the parking lot."

activity: getting a first part-time job
story:
The automatic doors at Halloran's Grocery exhaled cold air every time they opened, and by her third loop of the produce section Claire had learned to time her nerves to them. She had come for an interview at four o'clock, and now it was four forty, and the assistant manager, a woman named Ms. Karimi, was still behind the customer service desk with a stack of paperwork, waving Claire over with two fingers.

"You're hired if you want it," Ms. Karimi said, sliding a folder across the counter. "Weekends and two evenings. Bagging, stocking, carts when it's slow. Minimum wage, direct deposit if you want it. The only thing standing between you and a name tag is this." She tapped the top sheet, which was dense with boxes and numbered lines, and then she was called away to a register that had begun flashing.

Claire stared at the form. At the top, in bold letters, it said Employee's Withholding Certificate, and beneath that, Form W-4, Department of the Treasury. She had expected an emergency contact sheet, maybe a dress code. Instead there were steps, allowances, a place to claim dependents she did not have. Around her the store went on: mist hissing over the lettuce, a cart with one bad wheel rattling past, the PA announcing a spill in aisle nine.

She took out her phone and texted her mother: "I got it?? But there's a tax form. I don't know what to put." Her mother was at work and slow to answer, so Claire carried the folder to the break room doorway, where Kianna, who had worked here since junior year, was taping a birthday-cake sign to the wall. Kianna's whole ambition this summer was to be made shift lead, and she was adorning every surface of the store as if diligence could be measured in tape.

"Is it hard?" Claire asked, holding up the form.

"Everyone freezes on it," Kianna said, climbing down from the step stool. "It's a Form W-4. You fill it out so they know how much federal income tax to take out of each paycheck." She said it briskly, the way she said everything, and went back to her sign, which was slightly crooked and which she adjusted three times.

Claire sat on a crate by the loading door, where the smell of cardboard and cold cantaloupe mixed with the heat blowing in from the lot. Her mother's reply finally arrived: "Single, one job, just you. Put your signature at the bottom and take a picture of it before you hand it in." Then a second message, longer, in which her mother reminisced about her own first job at a dry cleaner and how she had felt, at eighteen, that filling out official paper made her a person the government could see. Claire read it twice. It was the closest thing to a letter she had gotten in years, and she decided not to say so, in case saying it would stop her mother from ever doing it again.

She filled in the boxes slowly, printing her address, checking the box for single, leaving the dependent line blank because there was no one to list. Some of it still felt equivocal to her, boxes whose consequences she couldn't see, a whole system of withholding she understood only as a shape. She thought of her economics teacher, who liked to say that a person could be a savant about markets and still misjudge their own budget, and how her mother would say the opposite, that you learned money by earning it, not by theorizing. Both of them were probably right, and neither was going to stand behind this counter at five o'clock with her name on a badge.

She photographed the completed form, signed it, and carried it back to the desk. Ms. Karimi returned, glanced it over, and slid a plastic sleeve across the counter. Inside was a name tag with CLAIRE printed in blue capitals, slightly crooked, like Kianna's sign.

"Wear it Saturday, six a.m.," Ms. Karimi said. "And tell your friend back there the shift lead decisions come out next week, if she ever stops decorating long enough to hear it."

Kianna, who had absolutely heard it, dropped her roll of tape.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
story:
Jonathan had signed up for the Saturday shift at the community garden's food bank table because his mother said it would look good on applications, and he had said "sure" with the enthusiasm of a boy agreeing to a dentist appointment. The garden sat behind the rec center, eight raised beds and a shed with a mural of a sunflower on it, and the food bank table operated out of a folding canopy where Mr. Goh, a retired pharmacist with reading glasses pushed up into his gray hair, sorted crates of produce with an atavistic suspicion of anything soft.

"You're Jonathan," Mr. Goh said, handing him a crate of squash. "The one who came to expiate his college applications."

"That's not what I said on the form."

"It's what the form meant." Mr. Goh held up a zucchini, squeezed it, and set it in a discard bin with ceremony, like a judge sentencing a repeat offender.

Rebeka arrived ten minutes late with a canvas bag and a paper hat from the burger place on Delmore, her shift having just ended. Grady came with her, because Grady came with everything Rebeka did, carrying a thermos he referred to as "the good coffee" and refusing to share it, which was his one consistent personality trait. The four of them arranged the crates under the canopy: squash, apples somebody's tree had overproduced, bread from the bakery that had gone out of business the month before, and, inexplicably, forty pounds of onions.

The bread was the problem. Rebeka, untying her paper hat, mentioned that her manager threw out three garbage bags of unsold buns every night, and Mr. Goh made a sound like a kettle. He asked whether her manager knew stores and restaurants could donate without being sued, and Rebeka said no, he thought if somebody got sick off an old bun, the restaurant would be finished. Mr. Goh said that was the whole point of the law, the Bill Emerson Good Samaritan Food Donation Act of 1996, which gives food donors limited protection from liability, and that was why places donated surplus food at all.

"So he's just scared of nothing," Rebeka said.

"He's scared of the thing he imagines," Mr. Goh said, "which is heavier than any real thing."

Jonathan, sorting apples by bruise, felt something shift in him that he distrusted on principle. He had spent the morning privately ranking volunteers by probable college essays, the way he ranked everything, and had put himself near the top on irony. But the law thing snagged him. At lunch he looked it up on his phone behind the onion crates, scrolling with a thumb sticky from apple juice, and found the act described in a government database with all the gravity of a document that had never once been read for fun. His erudition on the subject now extended to one page of a .gov website, which was, he conceded, one page more than Rebeka's manager had.

"He could just call the food bank," Jonathan said, when the lunch crowd had thinned. "They'd pick it up. He doesn't have to do anything but say yes."

"My manager doesn't say yes to anything," Rebeka said. "Last week he said no to a second mop bucket."

"The buns are already in bags," Grady said, from inside his thermos. "It's not like he'd have to touch them again. He's basically throwing away pre-packaged charity."

Rebeka looked at them both with the expression she used when boys were being slow and also, occasionally, right. "I'll ask him Monday," she said. "If he says no, you two are coming with me and explaining the liability thing, because when I say legal words he hears a fire alarm."

The afternoon rush came and went, a retired couple who took squash and complimented the sunflower mural, a man with a wheeled cart who discussed onions at a length Jonathan would not have believed possible, a woman who worked at the library and traded them a stack of novels for a bag of apples. Jonathan found he was good at the table, better than he expected, mostly because he could carry two crates and did not lecture anyone about kale. He had assumed volunteering would be a performance of goodness for an audience of admissions officers. It turned out to mostly be logistics, and the logistics turned out to be satisfying in a way he had no category for, which annoyed him.

By five they were folding the canopy and fighting over who had to take the onion crates back to the shed. Jonathan lost, or won, depending on how you felt about forty pounds of onions, and carried them across the grass while Rebeka walked backward in front of him doing a dramatic monologue about her manager's fears, pausing only to say "limited protection from liability" in a courtroom voice until Grady laughed so hard he sat down on a raised bed.

"You know I'm doing this for my resume," Jonathan said, setting the crates inside the shed door.

"Sure," Rebeka said. "And I'm asking my manager about the buns because I love buns."

"And the buns," said a voice from the shed, "are not going to throw themselves at the hungry."

Mr. Goh emerged with a rake and the reading glasses now on the end of his nose, and pointed it at the last crate still in the grass.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
story:
The argument started over a throw-in, of all things. Alec wanted the short throw, Ashton had already turned upfield, and by the time the ball went out of bounds again they were shouting at each other in voices that carried across the whole pitch. Kelly-Anne stood between them with her hands up, saying their names like she was calling dogs off a scent. In the third row of the bleachers a couple of freshmen went quiet and watched.

It had been building for weeks. The team had started the season politely, almost shyly, everyone passing to everyone and apologizing for mistakes they hadn't made. Then somewhere in the middle of October the politeness curdled, and every frustration, every swallowed grievance about playing time and lazy recovering runs, coagulated into something you could practically see at practice, a gray weight sitting in the middle of the field.

At the end of that session Ms. Leung blew her whistle and made them sit on the balls. She was a chemistry teacher who coached soccer because nobody else would, and she had a way of looking at a group that made the group look at itself. "A psychologist named Bruce Tuckman proposed in 1965 that groups develop through four stages," she said. "Forming, storming, norming, performing. You're storming. It's normal." Then she told them to run a cool-down lap and went to collect the cones.

Ashton ran the lap thinking about it. He hadn't known there was a word for what was happening to them, let alone a sequence, let alone someone who had thought about it in 1965 and decided it applied to more than soccer teams. That night he looked it up at the kitchen table while his mother washed dishes, and he read the stage names twice, forming, storming, norming, performing, and felt something loosen in his chest. It wasn't that they were falling apart. It was that they were on schedule.

The problem was Alec. Alec had done the reading too, or enough of it, and had decided that since the storming was normal, his part in it required no apology. "It's literally a stage," he said the next day, lacing his cleats on the bench. "I'm being a stage." Kelly-Anne said that was the stupidest thing she'd ever heard him say, which launched a fresh argument that Ashton, for once, watched from a distance, like a man standing in a doorway out of the rain.

He tried to think it through honestly. He liked the idea of stages because it promised an ending: storm, then norm, then perform, a line drawn forward through the season. But a sequence wasn't a guarantee, and nothing in what he'd read said a team had to reach the last stage at all. The etiology of their trouble wasn't mysterious, either. It was Alec wanting to be scouted, and Kelly-Anne wanting to win the district title her sister had never won, and Ashton wanting both of those people to still like him in November. A theory could name a stage. It couldn't make anyone pass the ball.

The semifinal came on a cold Tuesday, the kind of night when the floodlights made halos and breath hung over the field like something the grass was giving off. They were losing one to nothing at half, and in the huddle Kelly-Anne said, quietly, that she was done talking about Tuckman. Then, eleven minutes into the second half, Alec took the ball down the left side and, instead of shooting from an angle he'd been hogging all season, cut it back across the box. Ashton was there. The goal was almost silent, the net barely moving, and the lead they took three minutes later was evanescent, undone by a rebound before the crowd had finished celebrating the first.

They went to penalties, and Ashton, who had drawn the last kick out of the hat at practice that morning, stood over the ball with the whole gray weight of the season behind him. He thought, absurdly, of Ms. Leung stacking cones. He thought of the word norming, and how he still couldn't have said whether this was it, whether they had passed through anything at all or simply gotten tired of shouting. The keeper shifted his weight. Ashton exhaled and started his run.

activity: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
story:
Anais spread the pamphlets across the kitchen table at eleven minutes past eight, with Reanna due at half past and the presentation due first period tomorrow. Ms. Petrov had assigned it on Monday: fifteen minutes on consent, contraception, and where to get tested, delivered to the rest of the peer health class, and Anais had volunteered before she understood what volunteering would cost her.

She exhumed her notes from the bottom of her backpack, where they had spent four days under a gym shirt and a ruined pen. The top page was smeared. The second page held her only solid research, a clinic handout with a statistic highlighted in green, and she read it again while the kettle worked itself toward a whistle.

Reanna came in through the back door without knocking, which was the arrangement. "My mom's still at the courthouse," Anais said. "She's got a deposition tomorrow, so she's reading transcripts at the table like it's the end of the world. We're in the kitchen."

"Fine by me. The kitchen has food." Reanna pulled a stool to the counter and looked at the pamphlets. "So you actually have to say words out loud. To people. About this."

"Kaleb's coming too. He said he'd be the audience so I can practice on someone who won't laugh."

"Kaleb laughs at everything."

"He laughs after, not during. There's a difference."

Kaleb arrived at ten to nine with a bag of clementines and took the chair nearest the auxiliary door, the one that let a draft in whenever the wind came off the school field. Anais stood where the refrigerator handle wouldn't block her, held her smeared notes at an angle she could read, and began.

"Consent has to be freely given, and you can take it back at any point, even in the middle. If someone's been drinking, they can't give it. Silence isn't it. Going along with something because you're scared isn't it." She kept her eyes on the microwave clock. "That part's fine. That part I can say in my sleep."

"Say the pill part," Reanna said, peeling a clementine. "That's the part you keep skipping."

"I don't skip it. I say the pill exists and move on, because the pill part is where I sound like an idiot."

"You don't sound like an idiot. You sound like a person who's never taken it, which you are. So learn the numbers and say the numbers."

Anais put the notes down and picked up the clinic handout. "Fine. Here's what I've got. With typical use, about seven in a hundred people relying on the combined pill for a year have an unintended pregnancy." She said it flat, the way the handout said it, and watched their faces to see if it landed. "Typical use. Not perfect use. Typical, meaning people like everybody actually is."

"Seven out of a hundred," Kaleb repeated. "That's more than I thought."

"That's why the nurse at the clinic kept saying set a phone reminder for the same time every day. I kept wondering why she hammered it so hard. Then I found this and it made sense, kind of. People miss doses." Anais paused. "I can't explain the biology of why missing doses matters. I asked my mom and she got weird about it and started talking about her deposition instead."

"You don't have to explain the biology," Reanna said. "You just have to say the number and say the reminder thing. Say: with typical use, about seven in a hundred people on the combined pill for a year have an unintended pregnancy, often because doses are missed. Then say, so if someone's on it, a daily alarm isn't fussiness, it's the whole system working."

Anais wrote that on the back of the handout, word for word, because it was better than anything on her smeared pages.

"Now the clinic part," Kaleb said. "Where do people even go?"

"There's the health department on Corbett Street. You can walk in. Testing for infections is free, and it's confidential, which means they don't call your parents, even at sixteen." She had checked this twice by phone, disguising her voice slightly the first time and then not bothering the second. "You don't need money and you don't need a reason. You can just go once a year, like a checkup."

"Are you going to say that part from experience?" Reanna asked.

"No. I'm going to say it because I called and asked, and that's what I'll tell people if they ask. I'm not going to pretend I've done it. I'll say, here's the address, here's the hours, here's what happens when you walk in. And if someone asks me something I don't know, I'll say I don't know and write it down and find out."

Kaleb peeled another clementine and split it in three without being asked. "That's actually a better presentation than pretending," he said. "Half the adults who come talk to us pretend."

Anais ran the whole thing once more, start to finish, while Reanna acted out an audience member who asked annoying questions and Kaleb kept time. Eleven minutes. She cut nothing and added the phone reminder line in the contraception section, where it belonged, and her voice only caught once, on the word confidential.

At ten o'clock her mother came in for water, transcripts under her arm, and stood at the counter listening for a moment without saying anything.

"Seven in a hundred," her mother said finally. "With typical use?"

"That's what the clinic handout says."

Her mother filled her glass and went back down the hall, and Anais squared the pamphlets into a stack, put the handout with its green highlight on top, and set the phone alarm for six.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
story:
The Salazars' den smelled like burnt popcorn and jalapeño chips, and Addison had claimed the good beanbag chair before anyone else thought to, which was the kind of tactical achievement her brother would spend the whole night trying to reverse. Twelve people had squeezed in around the Huddens' television because the Huddens had the biggest screen on the block, and also because the Huddens had left for the weekend and given the key to Addison's father, who had opened the door and said, "Enter freely," in his Dracula voice, which never got less stupid and somehow never got old.

The game had been lopsided for three quarters, which was why nobody minded when Marissa started rooting for the away team's point guard, a lanky kid named Dawes who had hit two shots in a row and then, absurdly, a third. "He's heating up," Marissa announced, standing in front of the nachos. "Give him the ball. He's getting hot."

"Two threes," said Justine from the couch, without looking up from the score app on her phone. "That's a streak of two. My grandmother does better at the casino and we don't call her hot, we call her lucky."

"My grandmother is hot," Addison's brother said, and was pelted with popcorn, and the room settled into the comfortable murmur of a game where the outcome no longer mattered and the arguing could. Dawes missed a runner in the lane. Justine raised both fists like she'd won a debate. Marissa said the miss proved nothing because the shooter had been fouled, which the referee, a man both girls now held in personal contempt, had apparently not noticed.

Mr. Islam, the neighbor from two doors down who came to these things for the guacamole and stayed for the arguments, leaned back in the recliner. "The hot hand," he said, in the tone of a man laying down a card. "My father used to say the hot hand is the biggest lie in sports. He had a book of aphorisms. Feed a cold, starve a fever. Never trust a streak. That one was his."

Adisson had been half-listening, but the phrase snagged in her, the way a loose thread snags. Somewhere in the back of her mind there was a shelf, and on that shelf was a video she'd watched at one in the morning in October, recommended by an algorithm that knew her too well. Gilovich, Vallone and Tversky, 1985. They'd called the hot hand an illusion. That part she'd absorbed while brushing her teeth. But there was a second shelf, a lower one, and on it something about a flaw. "Wait," she said out loud, lifting a hand like she was in class. "Wait, wait. Don't fight yet."

The room looked at her. On the screen, Dawes hit another three, and the crowd noise swelled, transfiguring the den for a second into something almost religious, everyone's faces lit and yelling. Addison talked over it, fast, because she could feel the memory dissolving. "Okay. So there was this study, 1985, Gilovich, Vallone and Tversky, and they said the hot hand is an illusion. Like, just randomness, people seeing patterns. That's the classic thing, that's what everybody learned."

"Justine's side," her brother said, and Justine bowed.

"But," Addison said, and held up her second finger, "hold on, because I watched this whole video about it and I fell asleep during the boring part and then rewatched it, so I know it. In 2018, Miller and Sanjurjo reanalyzed it and found a statistical flaw in the original, and actual evidence of streak shooting. So the hot hand is real. Sort of. Partly." She paused, aware that she had reached the end of what she could defend. "The math part of the flaw I cannot explain, because the video lost me there, and I will not pretend otherwise."

Marissa made a sound like a courtroom lawyer who has just been handed the winning document. Justine made a sound like the other lawyer. Mr. Islam dipped a chip with great dignity and said, "Two sides of one coin, and the coin is still spinning," which Addison privately found less trenchant than he clearly did. Her father shouted that everyone under twenty had to surrender their phones to verify nothing, the whole point of a watch party being to argue from the heart.

By the fourth quarter Dawes had hit five of his last seven, and Marissa was insufferable, doing a small dance by the television, and Justine had gone quiet in a way that Addison recognized as recalculating rather than conceding. Addison sat in her beanbag with the nacho cheese cooling on her fingers and held both truths like two cards she refused to discard. The streak was probably partly real and partly luck and there was no clean line between them, and the boring part of the video was the part that would have told her where the line was, if she ever bothered to watch it a third time. She thought she might. She thought she might not.

With four seconds left and the game decided either way, Dawes took one more shot from somewhere near the logo, deep and unnecessary and gorgeous, and the whole den rose up off the furniture at once as it banked in.

"See," Marissa screamed over the buzzer. "SEE."

"Two out of three," Justine said grimly, and reached for the last chip.

story:
Sara sat cross-legged on the kitchen floor the night before Eid, counting out envelopes while her mother measured rice into plastic bags. There were seven bags, one for each person in the house, and Sara wrote the names on little slips in her looping handwriting: Ammi, Abu, herself, her three little brothers, and Dadi, who was asleep already with the fan pointed at her feet. Her mother checked the measure twice, then a third time, because it had to be the same for everyone, a set amount, not what anyone felt like giving that day.

"It has to be given before the prayer tomorrow," her mother said, sealing the last bag. "Not after. If it comes after, it's just a gift."

Sara stacked the bags in a crate by the door. "What's it called again?"

"Zakat al-fitr," her mother said, already looking for the tape. "Per person, for every member of the family."

Sara had known about it her whole life without ever really holding it in her hands before. In previous years it had been a thing her parents did on their phones, a transfer made in the middle of cooking, an errand her father ran after the night prayer while she argued with her brothers over who got the good kurta pressed first. This year her mother had handed her the measuring cup and said, you're eighteen, you do it, and the weight of the rice in her palm had surprised her, the way a thing can be ordinary for years and then suddenly specific.

The Eid prayer was held in the big public park off Chandler Road, because the mosque three towns over couldn't hold everyone and the city granted a kind of informal clemency every year, waiving the usual permits so that blankets and prayer rugs could be laid out on the soccer field before the sun got high. Sara's family arrived early, the crate of rice bags riding on her hip. The grass was still wet and cold through her sandals, and men in white and women in pale colors were arranging themselves in rows near the treeline, and somewhere behind her a boy was shouting that he'd found a perfect spot by the swings.

That was where Payton and Kayleb found her. They had come to the park for entirely different reasons, Payton to run the trail loop and Kayleb because Payton had the car keys, and they'd wandered over when they saw the crowd. Payton worked at the smoothie shop near school and had once defended Sara's fasting to a customer who complained that Sara's slowness at the blender was proof of something. Kayleb was acerbic about nearly everything, and he did not make an exception for religion.

"So what's the rice for," he said, nodding at the crate. "Picnic?"

"It's zakat al-fitr," Sara said. "Before the Eid prayer, everyone who can afford it gives it, a set amount for each person in the family. So that poor families can celebrate Eid too." She said it plainly, the way her mother said it, and then felt the strange doubling of hearing her own voice carry the sentence, like the words had been sitting in her chest all night waiting for somewhere to go.

"An entry fee," Kayleb said. "Nice. The whole thing's a system to subjugate people into giving, and everyone just calls it beautiful."

"It's not to subjugate anyone," Sara said, and heard her own sharpness. "Nobody's making us. My mom measured it out three times because she wanted it to be right."

Payton was quiet, watching a man near the collection tables lifting a girl onto his shoulders so she could see over the crowd. Sara followed her gaze and saw that the tables were already piled with rice and flour and sealed envelopes, families streaming past them in their good clothes, each dropping something into the bins before finding their places in the rows. The whole field was doing it, hundreds of households, before the prayer, exactly as her mother had insisted, and she understood suddenly that the order wasn't a rule for its own sake, that it was timed so the food would arrive before the day of feasting began, so that whoever received it would have it on the day itself.

"I don't know," she said, more slowly, because Kayleb was looking at her like he wanted a fight and she didn't want to give him one that she'd lose by winning. "Maybe it can be a system and still be beautiful. Maybe the system is what makes sure the beautiful part actually reaches people instead of just being a feeling." She shifted the crate on her hip. "It doesn't fix anything permanent. It's one day. I don't know what the poor do the day after Eid, and I don't think anyone at that table knows either."

Kayleb shrugged, but he didn't answer, and Payton said the prayer was starting, and the three of them drifted toward the edge of the field where the non-praying could stand without being in the way. Sara carried the crate to the collection table and counted the bags into a volunteer's waiting arms, seven, and the volunteer, an older woman with henna to her wrists, touched each bag as though counting them back, as though the number mattered as much as the rice.

The prayer ended and the field broke apart into hugging and shouting and children racing toward the playground with coins in their fists. Sara's youngest brother barreled into her legs and demanded she come judge a race. She was halfway to the swings when she glanced back toward the collection tables, meaning only to find her mother in the crowd, and saw Kayleb standing at the end of the row of bins, alone, hastily dropping a folded bill through the slot of the box marked for cash donations, then shoving his hands in his pockets and walking off fast in the direction of the trail.

James's mother had volunteered him before she told him, which was how things usually worked. The Kwanzaa celebration had spilled out of the community hall onto Delancey Street, cordoned off between the shuttered laundromat and the arepa stand, and at six o'clock, when the sun was already gone, he was supposed to stand at the small stage near the kinara and explain the day's principle to the gathered families. He had said yes the way you say yes to a mother holding a tray of cassava, and then he had spent the walk over rehearsing what he thought he knew, which was that Kwanzaa was an old tradition, something carried from Africa across the ocean, older than anyone could remember.

Evan found him behind the stage, where James was pretending to straighten a folding table. Evan had come for the food, honestly, and said so, being voluble as ever about the plantains he'd already eaten two of and intended to eat six more of. When James told him what he was about to do, Evan pulled a creased flyer from his jacket pocket, the kind the woman at the welcome table had been handing out all evening, and held it under the string of lights.

"You should read this before you go up there," Evan said. "Seriously."

James read it standing in the cold, his breath fogging the paper. The words did not say what he had planned to say. Kwanzaa had been created in 1966, by a man named Maulana Karenga, and it ran from December 26 to January 1. It honored seven principles, one each day, beginning with Umoja. Not ancient. Not carried across any ocean. Invented in California within his own grandmother's lifetime, on purpose, the way someone builds a house on purpose.

"Wait," James said. "It's newer than my mom."

"Newer than my dad," Evan said. "Practically an affidavit, that flyer. It's got citations."

James sat down on an overturned milk crate. His speech, the one he had been rehearsing since Tuesday, was now a speech about something that did not exist. He could feel it dissolving, and underneath the panic something more uncomfortable: the question of whether it mattered. People at this festival had been lighting the candles for years, his family among them. His aunt made the necklaces. His little cousins argued over who got to place the ears of corn. If all of it had started in 1966, in a room with someone deciding, did that make it thinner? He had always quietly assumed that older meant truer, that people valorize whatever came before them simply because it came before, and now the ground under that assumption was moving.

Ariana appeared with two cups of ginger beer and gave him one without asking. She was better at this than he was; her family hosted the December 26 dinner every year, and she had recited principles in front of relatives since she was nine. When he told her about the flyer, she shrugged.

"So it was made," she said. "So what. Somebody made your jacket too and you still wear it."

"That's different."

"Why, because nobody gave a speech about your jacket?"

She said it lightly, but it landed somewhere serious. James looked out at the street, at the candles guttering in glass jars along the curb, at the drum circle starting up unevenly near the arepa stand, at Ms. Wiśniewski from the chemistry department at the college standing with her plate, nodding along though she surely didn't know the songs. Everyone here was keeping something alive on purpose. Maybe the purpose was the tradition. Maybe it didn't need to be old to be real, but he wasn't certain, and he didn't think pretending to be certain would help.

"Umoja," he said to Ariana, testing it. "That's tonight. Day one."

"Umoja means unity," she said. "You knew that."

He had known it and not known it, the way you know a word before you ever ask where it came from. His mother leaned around the stage curtain and pointed at her watch, and James stood, took the flyer with him, and folded it into his back pocket. He walked out past the curtain, and the little crowd turned toward him, maybe forty people, breath rising, the kinara behind him with one green candle waiting to be lit after the black one.

"Kwanzaa started in 1966," James said, and heard his own voice steadier than he expected. "A man named Maulana Karenga created it. It goes from December 26 to January 1, and every day has its own principle. Seven of them, one each day. Tonight is the first, and it's the one I was asked to talk about." He paused, and Ariana, in the second row, raised her cup an inch. "Umoja. Unity. Which is easy to say and harder to do, and I'm still working on what it's asking of us, but I think the working is part of it."

His mother lit the candle. Somewhere behind him the drum circle caught a rhythm and held it.

story:
Jonathan had never seen Ms. Silva's living room so full. The whole block had migrated there for the championship because she had the biggest television and the only basement that didn't flood, and now the couch, the stairs, and the carpet were occupied by parents and kids shouting at the same screen. His father sat in the armchair with a paper plate balanced on his knee, and Isla had claimed the spot directly in front of the TV, arms crossed, wearing the opposing team's colors like a dare.

The fourth quarter was tied when the running back stretched for the end zone and the pile collapsed on top of him. The officials convened for a long time, and when the head referee raised both arms, the basement erupted. His father stood up so fast the plate went spinning onto the carpet. Jonathan joined the cheering because that was what you did, but he hadn't actually seen the ball. Nobody had. The camera angle had been blocked by three hundred pounds of tackler.

"Show it again," the coach from two doors down shouted at the screen, as if volume were a remote control. "They have to show it again. That's the whole point of television." Several people agreed loudly. Isla did not cheer; she stood with her hand over her mouth, and Jonathan understood that she had not seen the ball either, and that her silence was its own kind of honesty.

It came to him then, a fact he had picked up in Ms. Silva's media studies elective, of all places, buried in a unit he'd assumed would be boring. He had written it on an index card for a quiz and thrown the card away. Now it surfaced whole. "The first instant replay ever on TV was CBS, during the Army-Navy game, December 7, 1963," he said, and the room quieted enough that he kept going. "A director named Tony Verna devised the system." He hadn't planned to say it out loud; it just seemed important, suddenly, that people yelling for technology to settle their argument should know where the technology came from.

"1963," his father repeated, in the tone he used when he thought Jonathan was showing off. "Fascinating. Now can they show the play." On the screen, they did. The broadcast cut to a replay from the sideline, and the basement leaned forward as one consciousness, every separate opinion suddenly fused into a single held breath. The angle was clean this time. The ball was visible, and it was short of the goal line by what looked like half a football, and then the runner's knee was down.

For a moment nobody said anything. Then the referee appeared on screen and announced, almost apologetically, that the ruling on the field was reversed. Touchback. No touchdown. Ms. Silva's basement divided along its fault line with a speed that would have impressed a geologist: the home side groaning, Isla's small contingent suddenly alive, his father dropping back into the armchair like a man shot.

"The replay's rigged," the coach said. "They slow it down, they pick the angle, they make it look like whatever they want." He was already half out the door for the porch and his cigarettes, but Jonathan followed him, partly to get away from the noise and partly because the accusation bothered him in a way he couldn't immediately name. "It's the same footage," Jonathan said on the porch steps. "They just showed the one clean angle. It's not grandiose conspiracy stuff. The ball was short." The coach exhaled smoke and looked at him with something between affection and pity, the look adults give you when they've decided you'll understand when you're older. "The footage doesn't lie," he said. "The people choosing the footage aren't the footage."

Jonathan stood there while the cold worked into his jacket. He tried to dichotomize it in his head, the way he did for essays: replay good, human judgment bad, technology neutral, humans corrupt. But it kept refusing to sort. The machine had shown the truth and the truth had been reached through a director's choice, the same kind of choice Tony Verna had made in 1963 when he decided the moment was worth repeating. The tool and the hand holding the tool were tangled together, and Jonathan couldn't cleanly praise one and blame the other, and he wasn't sure anyone could.

Inside, the game went on without the touchdown, and the home team lost by a field goal as the clock ran out. Isla found him in the kitchen afterward, where he was helping Ms. Silva stack cups he didn't feel like stacking. "Nice history lesson," she said, and he braced for mockery. "Verna. December 7, 1963. That was actually kind of great." She took the cups from his hands and set them in the sink. "Of course, if the replay had gone the other way, you'd all be calling it the greatest invention in sports."

"That's the thing," Jonathan said. "I'd want to believe it was neutral. I just don't think it is." Isla considered this, drying her hands on her jeans, and Ms. Silva turned off the television in the other room so that the house went quiet except for the ice melting in the punch bowl. "Come on," Isla said finally, nodding toward the door where his father stood waiting, staring at the dark screen. "You can tell him the truth was short by half a football. See how far that gets you." Jonathan pulled on his jacket and followed her out into the cold.

story:
The calculus room still smelled of the floor wax the custodian had put down over the weekend, and Samuel sat in the second row with the box problem in front of him, unsolved for three days. A rectangular sheet of cardboard, twenty centimeters by thirty, square corners cut out, folds up into an open box; find the size of the squares that maximizes the volume. He had written V equals x times the quantity thirty minus two x times the quantity twenty minus two x, multiplied it out into a cubic, and then stopped, because he did not yet know what to do with a cubic.

Mr. Ahmed had put the problem on the board Friday and said only, "You have everything you need." Samuel doubted this. He had pages in his notebook that argued otherwise.

Dakota slid into the seat beside him and looked at his page. "Still stuck on the box?"

"I can get the polynomial," Samuel said. "I can't get the peak of it. I could graph it and zoom in forever, but that's cheating. It's not an answer, it's an approximation of an answer."

"Graphing is how everybody did it for two hundred years," Dakota said. "Before the algebra, I mean."

"That's supposed to comfort me?"

Bruce arrived late, as always, garrulous even at eight in the morning, narrating his walk from the parking lot, the ice on the steps, the janitor who had waved at him with a mop. He dropped his bag and leaned over Samuel's other shoulder. "Oh, the box. I did the box. You want the derivative."

"I know I want the derivative. The section on derivatives is next week. That's the whole problem."

Bruce pulled the textbook from his bag, flipped ahead to a chapter they had not been assigned, and turned it so Samuel could see. The pages were dense with expressions Samuel half recognized: polynomials, then those same polynomials with something written beside them, something that looked like a fraction. d y over d x. The numerator and denominator sat apart, stacked like an actual ratio, and yet the text treated them as a single mark, one symbol with two floors.

"Why does the book write it like a fraction," Samuel asked, "if it isn't one? You can't cancel anything. You can't clear the denominator. It's just lying there."

"That's Leibniz," Bruce said. "The notation dy/dx comes from Gottfried Leibniz, and it's still the standard in mathematics today." He tapped the page. "Mr. Ahmed went on about it Tuesday, when you were at the orthodontist. He said other people invented the same ideas at the same time with different symbols, but this is the one that survived."

Samuel looked at the mark again. It behaved like a fraction and it didn't. It was a machine for stating how fast one thing changed against another, dressed in the costume of a ratio. He copied it into his notebook anyway, because whatever it was, it was the language the book spoke, and he could not afford to be an ideologue about notation when a problem was waiting.

Mr. Ahmed came in, set down his thermos, and saw the textbook open to the wrong chapter. He did not close it. He wrote Samuel's polynomial on the board, the cubic from the box, and said, "Who can tell me where this is biggest?"

Dakota said, "You graph it."

"You graph it. Good. What does the graph do at the top of the hill?" Mr. Ahmed put the chalk against the board and drew the curve with his hand, a long rise, a rounded crest, a fall. At the crest he stopped. "Here. What is the slope here, exactly?"

Nobody answered. Samuel looked at the flat instant at the top, that single moment where the climb had ended and the descent had not begun, and said, "Zero."

"Zero. The slope is zero. And the derivative tells you the slope. So if you can find the derivative of your polynomial, and find where it equals zero, you have found your maximum." He set the chalk down. "Now, the rules for finding it. There are three, and they are shorter than you expect."

He taught the power rule in eleven minutes. Bring the exponent down, reduce it by one, term by term, each term subsumed into the new expression without ceremony. Samuel followed the cubic through the transformation, watching it lose a degree, and came out with a quadratic. He set the quadratic equal to zero, factored it on his own paper, and got two answers: x equals three and x equals eleven.

"Two answers," he said to Dakota. "Two squares I could cut."

"Two flat spots," Dakota said. "The hill goes up, flattens, goes up again or goes down, flattens, goes down. Only one of them is the top."

"One of them is a valley." Samuel went back to the original polynomial and evaluated it, no derivative now, just arithmetic. At three, the volume came out to eighteen hundred and thirty-two. At eleven, the side lengths went negative, the volume came out negative, and a negative volume meant nothing you could fold out of cardboard. He wrote 3 beside the crest of his sketch and crossed out the eleven.

Mr. Ahmed was walking the rows. He stopped at Samuel's desk, looked at the factored quadratic, the two roots, the chosen one, and the volume checked by substitution. He put one finger on the page where Samuel had copied the stacked notation, the numerator over the denominator, the mark that was not a fraction.

"You asked why it looks like that," Mr. Ahmed said. It was not a question.

"It looks like something it isn't," Samuel said. "It looks like a fraction and it works like a rule. I don't know which one to trust."

"Trust what it does," Mr. Ahmed said. "You just did. The box has its maximum at three centimeters. Cut the corners at three." He moved on down the row.

Samuel squared his paper and wrote the answer at the top, then sat with the strange mark a moment longer, the d over the d, honest in the only way that mattered, which was that it got him to three. He still did not know why a fraction that wasn't a fraction had survived three centuries when cleaner symbols had not. He underlined the answer twice.

"Three centimeters," he said to Dakota, and drew the cardboard in his notebook, twenty by thirty, the little squares marked at each corner, waiting to be cut.
