activity: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
story:
The interfaith tent at the harvest festival smelled of fried dough and cardamom, and Ashley stood at the edge of it holding a photocopied page she had read eleven times since Tuesday. Mr. Lawson had proposed the debate himself: could a rule from an ancient text still bind people who lived three thousand years after it was written, and should anyone care? He had assigned her the verse and told her, with his usual judicious calm, that she had to argue from the text itself, not from what she wished it said. That was the hard part. She had opinions. What she needed was evidence.

She had found the evidence on the photocopy, though it had taken her three readings to see it was evidence at all. The verse, Leviticus 19:9 and 10, told farmers not to reap all the way to the corners of their fields, and to leave the fallen gleanings where they lay, for the poor and the stranger. It was a rule about edges. It never said give charity, exactly. It said leave something unreaped, something inconvenient, on purpose, in the margins.

"So your rule is about farming," Jose said, leaning against the tent pole with a cup of cider. "Look around, Ashley. Bouncy castle. Kettle corn. The closest thing to a field is the parking lot." He was her assigned opponent and her friend in roughly equal measure, which made the whole thing harder. "Nobody here reaps anything. Rule's dead. Text it a eulogy."

"That's the lazy version," Ashley said, and immediately regretted the sharpness, because it sounded less like an argument and more like a peccadillo of her own temper. She softened it. "It says the poor and the stranger. That's who it's for. The field is just where the food was. If the food's somewhere else now, the rule follows the food."

Quinlan appeared with a clipboard, because Quinlan never went anywhere without a clipboard, and announced that the debate would happen at four, in front of the folding chairs, and that Mr. Lawson would judge. Ashley spent the next hour walking the festival grounds, which is what she did instead of rehearsing. She passed the embroidered vestments in the heritage hall, the drum circle that had debilitated into a rhythm nobody could follow once one drummer left, and the food stalls, where a woman was sliding unsold loaves into a crate at the end of the bread table.

"Those going to the dumpster?" Ashley asked.

"Cornerstone Shelter, six o'clock, every night of the festival," the woman said. "We bake too much on purpose. My mother taught it. She called it gleaning, the leftover part."

Ashley stood very still. She had been prepared to argue that the rule could translate, in theory, by analogy, with the appropriate humility about metaphor. She had a whole paragraph about agricultural societies and their equivalents. What she had not been prepared for was the rule standing in front of her in a crate, smelling of rosemary.

At four, the folding chairs filled more than anyone expected, maybe twelve people, maybe fifteen. Jose went first and was good, in his loose, amused way. "An honest farmer followed that rule because his neighbors watched his corners," he said. "There is no field, no corner, no watcher. A modern person following an ancient rule is like wearing someone else's glasses. You can do it, but you're guessing at the prescription."

Ashley had written an opening and abandoned it on the walk over. "The verse doesn't say donate," she said. "It says leave the corners unreaped and the fallen gleanings where they fall, for the poor and the stranger. It's a rule about not taking everything. It assumes you'll be tempted to take everything, and it builds the restraint into the harvest itself. The field changes. The temptation doesn't. The bread table here donates its extra loaves to the shelter every night, and they bake extra on purpose. That's the verse with a price tag instead of a shekel."

She heard Jose exhale beside her. She kept going, though her voice thinned. "What I can't settle is whether the rule binds anyone who doesn't accept the book. I think it binds the farmer who believes it. I think it only invites the rest of us. That's not a clean answer. It's the one the text gives."

Mr. Lawson was quiet for a moment, then said he would call it a draw, and Quinlan recorded it with visible dissatisfaction. Afterward the crowd dispersed toward the kettle corn, and Jose helped Ashley stack the chairs.

"So you win by finding the bread lady," he said. "That was luck, not argument."

"It was the argument," Ashley said. "I just found it before I could make it."

Jose hoisted the last chair onto the rack and grinned. "Then you owe me a rematch. Same rule, my side next time."

"Fine," she said, and handed him the photocopy, corners bent from her pocket. "Keep it. You'll need the edges."

story:
Mr. Eze's office smelled of coffee gone cold and the lemon polish he used on the same desk he'd had, he liked to say, since before Charles was born. Charles sat across from him with the deferral form unsigned in his lap, the paper warm where his hands had been holding it for ten minutes.

"You've read it three times," Mr. Eze said. "It hasn't changed."

"It pays real money. Two years at the firm, they cover the rest of tuition after." Charles turned the form over, though the back was blank. "My dad thinks I'd be insane not to take it. He'd have killed for that offer at eighteen."

"And your mother?"

Charles shrugged. "She said it's my decision, which from her means she hates it."

Mr. Eze leaned back. Outside the window, two juniors were dragging hurdles off the track, one of them Gwenyth, recognizable by the red jacket she wore in every season. Rim was probably at the benches with his headphones, waiting for her, waiting for Charles, waiting for the meeting to end so they could drive to the diner and argue about nothing. Charles had told them he'd have an answer by five.

"Can I tell you something my grandfather told me?" Charles said. "It's the only useful thing anyone's said all week, and it's not even about me."

"I'd like that."

"He went for his checkup last month, and he said the doctor spent half the time asking about habits. Whether he smoked, what he ate, how he slept. He thought it was strange, doctors prying like that, so he asked why, and the doctor told him about a study. The Framingham Heart Study. It started following residents of Framingham, Massachusetts in 1948, and it went on so long, tracking a whole town, that it gave medicine the term 'risk factor.' For habits and conditions that raise your risk of disease later on." Charles looked up. "My grandfather said that before that, doctors mostly waited until you were sick. The whole idea that you could look at what a person does now and see something about their future, that came from a study that ran for decades."

Mr. Eze was quiet for a moment, and Charles had the sense of being watched very carefully, the way his chemistry teacher used to watch a titration for the instant the pink would hold.

"So the deferral feels like a risk factor," Mr. Eze said. "A habit. A decision that predicts something twenty years out."

"I don't know if it does. That's the problem." Charles set the form on the desk, then picked it up again. "Gwenyth says I'm treating a job like it's a tattoo. Rim says everything is existentialism with me, that I think any choice ruins all the others. He said it to insult me, but it's kind of true. My grandfather's doctors aren't certain about any one person either, right? They just know what tends to happen. Tends. That's all anybody gets."

The hurdle crew had moved to the far curve of the track. Gwenyth stacked them in threes now, the same girl who in ninth grade couldn't carry her own backpack and used to make Rim do it. People changed under pressure that nobody could see happening. Charles wondered whether his grandfather, at the first exam in whatever year that was, had known he was becoming evidence.

"Here's what I keep going back and forth on," Charles said. "There's the way my dad thinks, which is take the sure thing, because the future is a wall and you should get what you can against it. And there's the way the study thinks, which is the future is more like a slope, and you can see where it's heading if you watch long enough. Those aren't the same future. If I sign, I'm betting on the wall. If I tear it up, I'm betting on the slope, on the idea that what I do at nineteen is a habit that compounds." He laughed, short and embarrassed. "Or maybe neither, and I'm just scared of both."

Mr. Eze slid a pen across the desk, not toward the form, just across, and left it in the middle. "I had a student once who deferred. He owns half of a company now. I had another who didn't, and he's the happiest man I know. I realize that's no help."

"It is, actually. It's honest." Charles took the pen. He held it over the signature line without touching down, watching his own hand as if it belonged to one of those other students, one of the futures in the slope that he couldn't see yet and never would, not fully, not until the years had already happened to him.

Gwenyth and Rim were walking toward the parking lot now, Gwenyth looking back at the building once.

Charles put the pen on the desk, folded the form in half, and stood. "Ask me again tomorrow," he said, and went out to meet them.

activity: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
story:
William had claimed the corner table by the periodicals an hour before closing, and he had spread his materials across it like evidence in a trial no one else knew was happening: the novel, a highlighted photocopy of chapter nine, and a half-finished essay that his teacher, Mr. Chowdhury, had returned with a single question penciled in the margin. "Who is telling you this, and why should you believe him?" The question had followed him out of the classroom and through the weekend, and now, on Sunday afternoon, he intended to answer it or at least to stop feeling ashamed of the B-minus.

The narrator in question was a man named Tulley, who spent the whole book insisting he had done nothing wrong. William had believed him on first read, which was the problem. In his essay he had written that the sister was cruel and the town was small-minded, exactly as Tulley reported them. Mr. Chowdhury's second note, further down the page, read: "Try rewriting one scene from the sister's point of view. Bring both versions on Tuesday."

Leonardo dropped into the chair opposite him with a stack of graphic novels and the particular energy of someone who wanted to be distracted. "You look morose," he said. "Chowdhury again?"

"He wants me to rewrite chapter nine from the sister's side. I don't get what that proves."

"Proves he can make you do work on a Sunday." Leonardo peeled open his first novel. "Francois is coming. He finished the book already, so he says."

Francois arrived ten minutes late, still in his soccer jacket, carrying nothing. He pulled the photocopy toward him without asking and read the margin notes upside down first, then right side up. "Tulley's a liar," he said. "Everyone in my class figured that out by chapter three."

"He's not a liar exactly," William said. "That's what I keep getting wrong. He lies to himself first. He leaves things out. He tells you what he saw and it's true, what he saw, but he only saw half of it." He heard his own voice speed up and slowed it. "That's the thing I can't put in the essay without it sounding like a book report."

Francois shrugged. "So a first-person narrator can only report what that one character sees, knows or chooses to say. A third-person omniscient narrator can reveal anyone's thoughts. Rewrite the scene third person and you'd get the sister's side and Tulley's, both."

William stared at him. "When did you become a pundit?"

"I read the handout. Twice. It's not the same as understanding it, which is why you're the one with the essay." He slid the photocopy back. "Do it. Five minutes. I want to see what happens."

So William wrote. He chose the scene where Tulley stands in the doorway while his sister packs a suitcase, and in the original Tulley notices only her coldness, her refusal to look at him, the loud shutting of drawers. William rewrote it from inside the sister's head, and the moment he did, the room filled with things Tulley had never mentioned: her hands shaking, her counting the money twice, her listening for the sound of the truck she already knew would not come. The coldness, seen from across the room, was fear. The drawers slammed because her fingers would not close softly.

"That's completely different," Leonardo said, reading over his arm. "Same room, same sister, different everything."

"And it's not even that she's more honest than he is," William said, writing fast now in the margin of his own essay. "She could be hiding things too. That's what omniscient buys you, both hides at once. First person, you get one set of eyes and one set of excuses." He looked up. "I don't know yet which version the author wants us to trust, or whether we're supposed to trust either. Maybe that's the actual question."

At the front desk, Mr. Chowdhury was checking in returns; William had not known the librarian worked Sundays until he glanced up and recognized him, and something in him decided not to waste the accident. He carried both versions of the scene to the desk and laid them side by side. "I rewrote it," he said. "First person and third. I'm still not sure what the book wants."

Mr. Chowdhury read neither page. He looked at the gap between them instead. "Bring the uncertainty with you on Tuesday," he said. "It's the most honest thing in your folder."

When William got home he wrote a short note and folded it into the front of his binder, addressed to himself, to be read before class: You believed Tulley the first time because he spoke first and he spoke in his own voice. Remember that the next voice you trust. Then he copied out the sister's paragraph one more time, because her hands were still shaking in it, and he wanted to make sure he had gotten that part exactly right. Outside his window the streetlight came on. He kept writing.

story:
The video arrived at 7:42 in the morning, while Paige was still eating toast over the sink. A warehouse fire, a wall of smoke, a caption in urgent capitals: THIS IS HAPPENING IN OUR CITY RIGHT NOW. Antoine had sent it to the group chat with three exclamation points, and Daria had already forwarded it to her cousin, who worked two streets over from where the smoke was supposedly rising.

By second period, the lab smelled the way it always did, like warm plastic and the lemon wipes the janitor used on the keyboards. Ms. Aydín had posted a new page on the class site, and Paige, who had finished her slideshow early, clicked on it mostly out of boredom. The page was plain, almost ugly: white background, black text, no graphics. It described a method attributed to an educator named Mike Caulfield, four moves you ran through before you shared anything. Paige read it twice.

"SIFT," she said to Daria, who had slid into the seat beside her, phone out, thumb already hovering over the forward arrow. "It's called SIFT. Stop, Investigate the source, Find better coverage, Trace claims to their original context."

"You made that up," Daria said.

"It's on the page. Look." Paige turned the monitor, but Daria was already holding out her phone, the fire video playing again, the smoke billowing in its little rectangle. Paige felt the pull of it herself, the way the image insisted on its own importance. A video seemed to reify the caption, to make it solid, as though seeing the smoke proved the smoke was where the caption said it was. But that was a veneer, she thought, a convincing surface over a gap nobody was checking. She had learned that word in English and never had a use for it until now.

"Stop," she said, mostly to herself, and put Daria's phone face down on the desk. Then she typed a frame from the video into the search bar, the image of the smoke plume against a water tower, and waited while the results loaded. The plough of the loading icon, the hum of thirty machines. The results came back in a quiet rush: the same frame, posted two years earlier, on a regional news site, in a city four hundred miles away, in a story about a factory fire that had injured no one. Daria leaned in and read the date aloud, then read it again, as though the numbers might rearrange themselves.

"That's not our water tower," Daria said slowly. "Ours doesn't have the stripe." She was canny that way, quicker than most people gave her credit for; she had simply never aimed that quickness at a video before. She picked her phone up off the desk and, for a moment, held it flat in both hands like something she wasn't sure she trusted herself to carry. Then she opened the group chat and typed, slowly, correcting herself twice, that the fire was old and far away, and that her cousin should stay put.

Paige found better coverage next, out of some stubbornness she couldn't quite explain, scrolling until she confirmed that nothing was burning in their city that morning, that the local paper's live feed was all road closures and a bake sale. It felt good, the checking. It also felt smaller than she had expected. She still didn't know who had taken the old clip and rewritten the caption, or why, or whether the person had meant to frighten anyone at all. That part stayed uncertain, and she let it stay.

Antoine appeared at her shoulder between classes, sheepish, holding his phone like an apology. "So I basically spread a fake fire," he said. "Cool. Great morning for me."

"You did the internet version of yelling fire in a crowded theatre," Daria said, and even he laughed, and for a second the three of them stood in the doorway of the lab, ordinary and relieved, the crisis shrunk to something they could carry.

Then Daria's phone buzzed, and her face changed, went bright and urgent. "Oh my God," she said. "Have you seen this? A shark on the highway. Everyone's saying it's real." Her thumb was already moving toward the forward arrow.

Paige reached over and pressed the phone gently back down toward the table. "Stop," she said.

activity: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
story:
Ashley had told Albert she'd done this before, which was true in the sense that she had once melted chocolate in a microwave and poured it over strawberries. That was the version of herself she preferred, the girl who knew her way around a kitchen, and she held to it now as she chopped a bar of dark chocolate on the cutting board, the knife ringing against the wood. The kitchen smelled faintly of the onions her mother had sautéed that morning, and the window over the sink was open to a July evening so humid the air felt like a held breath. She was making truffles for Melodie's going-away party, or that was the official reason; the unofficial reason was that she wanted to be the kind of person who made truffles.

"You said you've tempered chocolate," Albert said from the stool by the counter, watching her heap the chopped pieces into a steel bowl.

"I said I'd made chocolate. Tempering is just melting it carefully." She said it with the confidence of someone who had watched one video that afternoon and half of another. The video had been munificent with detail: seed the melted chocolate with a handful of unmelted bits, stir until they dissolved, watch the thermometer slide down to a temperature she could no longer remember. She stirred with a spatula, and the chocolate went glossy and loose, and she felt a warm certainty that she had a talent for this, that talent was simply a matter of deciding you had it.

Albert, who was better at chemistry than at pretending, had brought his notebook. "The cocoa butter forms different crystals," he said. "Only one of them is stable. If you get it right, it sets shiny and it snaps."

"Snap," Ashley repeated, pleased. She pressed a knife tip into a cooled smear on parchment and it broke with a clean, high click, like a small lock opening. She was so delighted that she declared victory early, dropped the truffles onto a plate, and slid the plate into the refrigerator, because in her mind a fridge was where finished things went to become more finished.

They left the kitchen and sat on the porch with Melodie, who was leaving in eleven days for a college none of them had visited, and the talk turned to whether people became themselves or were always themselves, Melodie arguing for the second with the cheerfulness of someone quoting a podcast. Albert called it determinism, everything caused by what came before, and Melodie said that if that were true she'd like to litigate it, and they laughed, and Ashley laughed too, though privately she sided with the idea that you could decide yourself into a new shape and have it hold, the way chocolate supposedly held a shape if you were careful. This was, she would later admit, an analogy she had made up evidence for.

Forty minutes later she carried the plate out of the refrigerator to show them, and the plate was cold, and the porch air was thick, and by the time she reached the steps the truffles had gone strange. Their surfaces were dulled, dusted with a dry, gritty white coating, like frost that had decided to be sand. She touched one and her fingertip came away powdery. "It's ruined," she said, and then, because she was not ready for it to be ruined, "It's still fine underneath. It's just cosmetic."

Albert took the plate and turned it in the light of the porch bulb, frowning at the haze. He looked it up on his phone while Melodie picked up a truffle and rubbed it with her thumb, the bloom smearing like chalk. "Sugar bloom," Albert read. "A dry, gritty white coating. It happens when moisture dissolves sugar on the chocolate's surface and the sugar recrystallizes as it dries." He glanced from the cold plate to the wet air and back, and Ashley understood it all at once and without anyone explaining further: the cold chocolate, the humid night, the dew that must have settled on the surface in the minute it took her to cross the yard. She had done this. She had made the frost herself, with the fridge and the evening and her own impatience.

She sat down on the step between them and ate the truffle anyway, and it was bitter and a little gritty on the first bite and then, underneath, perfectly smooth. Melodie asked whether she'd try again tomorrow, temper it properly, and Ashley said maybe, or maybe she'd let the fridge keep its opinions to itself. But later, after they'd gone, she stood in the kitchen with the window closed and the leftover chocolate hardening in its bowl, and she dipped her finger and wrote her name on the parchment, M-E-L, then stopped, and left it there to set.

activity: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
story:
The radiator in the computer lab clanked like something being executed, and Alicia decided that was a good omen, or at least a dramatic one, which in her experience portended nothing whatsoever except another afternoon in room 214. She had signed up for coding club because Ms. Saleh had said, with a straight face, that building software was "the closest thing to architecture that doesn't require a hard hat," and Alicia had wanted to believe her.

Her project that week was a small Java class called Student, with private fields and getter methods, and a test file that proved it worked. She had written the fields, made them private, and written the getters, and then she had written the test, and then she had stared at the screen with the particular blankness of a person who has done all the assigned steps and understood none of them.

"Your student has a name but no soul," said Melinda, sliding into the next chair with her own laptop balanced on a stack of outdated Java textbooks that the school kept the way museums keep armor, as a reminder that everything becomes obsolescent eventually. "Also your getter for age returns a String. Why."

"Because I panicked," Alicia said. "The number was being weird."

Melinda leaned over and did something fast. "Watch. I'm changing how your class stores the data. Instead of a name field and an age field, I'm going to keep one array of values and get them out by position. Don't argue, just watch."

"That sounds like vandalism."

"It's science."

Melinda rewrote the guts of the class, deleted name and age entirely, and rebuilt the getters to pull from her array instead. Then she ran Alicia's test file. Alicia, who had braced for a wall of red errors the way you brace for a fire alarm, watched every test pass. Nothing broke. Not one line of the test code had changed, and not one test had failed.

Alicia sat back. "Okay, that's creepy. You deleted my fields and my tests don't care?"

"Encapsulation means hiding a class's data behind methods, so other code can use the object without depending on how it stores its data," Melinda said, in the flat reciting voice she used for things she'd read off a poster in the hallway. Then, in her normal voice: "Which is why I can do this to you and you can't stop me."

"You could have led with that."

The sentence unlocked something older. Two years ago, before either of them had written a line of code, Alicia's mother had kept the family budget in a blue notebook, and when Alicia asked how much was left for shoes, her mother never handed over the notebook. She'd just say a number. Once Alicia had tried to read it directly, and her mother had covered the page with her hand and said, "You don't need my columns, you need my answer." Alicia had thought it was about privacy, control, the general parental allergy to being known. Now she understood it had also been a kindness. The answer stayed true even when her mother refinanced something and moved all the numbers to a spreadsheet. The rest of the family had gone on asking the same question and getting the same answer, never once seeing the machinery underneath. She said none of this to Melinda, though she did think, briefly and with pleasure, that her mother had been writing Java since before Java existed.

Ms. Saleh circulated with a mug that said WORLD'S ADEQUATE DEBUGGER, which she claimed she'd bought herself. She looked at Alicia's screen, at the array where fields used to be, and raised one eyebrow in a way that Alicia chose to interpret as approval.

"You let Melinda refactor you," Ms. Saleh said.

"She did it without asking."

"That's how you find out if your walls are real," Ms. Saleh said, and moved on before it could become a lesson, which Alicia appreciated.

That night Alicia opened her messages and found a note from Corey, who had missed club for a dentist appointment and wanted to know what he'd missed. She typed it as a message because Corey insisted that anything important be sent to him in writing, so he could reread it at two in the morning when his brain worked.

COREY: what happened at club, did anything good happen, was there drama

ALICIA: melinda deleted my fields and my tests still passed

COREY: that doesn't sound good

ALICIA: it is actually the whole point. other code talks to the getters, not to the data. so the inside can change and the outside doesn't care. I changed my mind about my mom a little

COREY: your mom was there?

ALICIA: no. long story. I'll explain tomorrow. bring snacks

COREY: always

She closed the laptop and thought about what she still didn't know, which was a lot, and felt, for once, fine about it. The test passing didn't mean her design was good, only that her walls held against one particular act of vandalism. Whether the walls were the right walls was a different question, one she'd have to answer by building more classes and letting more people break them.

The next afternoon Corey arrived with a bag of pretzels and an idea for a class of his own, and Alicia pulled her chair around so they could share one screen, and Melinda cracked her knuckles over the keyboard like a safecracker in a movie.

"Go ahead," Alicia said. "Try to break it."

activity: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
story:
The map on the wall of Mr. Tse's classroom showed the Atlantic as a lattice of arrows, red ones curling up the western edge and blue ones crawling south along the eastern shore. Grace copied them into her notebook before the bell finished ringing, because Mr. Tse had said on Monday that whoever could explain the arrows by Friday would present at the regional science symposium, and the symposium was in a hotel with a pool, and Grace had never stayed in a hotel with a pool.

She spread her copy out on the cafeteria table at lunch. "I think I have it," she said. "The red ones move fast. Look how long they are, and they're red, like speed, like heat from friction." She tapped the wide scarlet arrow leaving the Gulf. "So warm water races north, and that's why the red one reaches up past us."

Melody leaned over the notebook with her sandwich halfway to her mouth. Gregoire pulled the page closer, frowning. "The blue one off Greenland is long too," he said. "So the cold water races south at the same speed? Then what does the colour do?"

The question sat on the table between them. Grace looked at her own arrows and felt the small vertigo of a floor tilting. "Maybe length is speed," she said slowly, "and colour is something else."

"Colour is something else," Gregoire repeated, testing the sentence the way you test ice before stepping on it. He was the one who had first suggested red meant fast, two days ago, standing at the wall map with his finger on the Labrador coast, and Grace had been grateful for the theory because it catalyzed her whole understanding, had taken the vague dread of Friday and turned it into a plan.

After school she went back to the classroom, where Mr. Tse was stacking chairs. "I won't tell you," he said, which was his way of telling her nothing was broken yet. "But there's a reason the mapmakers gave you two variables instead of one." He left her alone with the wall.

She stood at the map for a long time, tracing arrows with her eyes instead of her finger because the laminated surface had a notice about fingerprints. The red arrows began in the tropics and ended off Norway. The blue arrows began in the Arctic and ended near Africa. She thought of the substrate of the map, the flat blue paper standing in for an ocean that was anything but flat, and thought about what a cartographer wants a sailor or a student to know at a glance. Not how fast. What temperature. She said it aloud to the empty room, quietly. "Warm currents are red arrows, cold currents are blue arrows." The colours were temperature, and she had been reading them as speed, and Gregoire had handed her the mistake in the first place, which meant she could hand it back.

On Thursday she found him at his locker. "I was wrong," she said. "It's not speed at all. Red is warm water, blue is cold. The Gulf Stream is warm, it carries heat north, and that's what keeps northern Europe milder than places at the same latitude. The arrows are temperature." She watched him take it in, watched the flicker of annoyance that precedes a person revising themselves in public. "So my long fast arrow," he said. "Is slow." He laughed, short and rueful. "My whole theory." She nodded, and did not say that his wrong theory had been the substrate her right one grew on, because that would have been generous in a way that cost her something, some share of the discovery she was not ready to surrender.

Melody came with her to watch the Friday presentation, and Mr. Tse signed the symposium form in blue ink that looked, on the page, exactly like cold water. In the hotel that weekend Grace stood at the edge of the pool at nine at night, alone, with the key card in the pocket of her robe. She had explained the map to forty strangers and answered every question, and one question still stuck in her like a splinter she couldn't find: how something as slow and scattered as a current could carry enough heat to change the climate of a whole continent, and whether the maps, with their clean red certainty, were telling her the truth or a convenient version of it. She stepped down into the shallow end, where the water was warm because the hotel kept it that way, and she stayed near the steps.

activity: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
story:
The video arrived at 9:14 on a Tuesday morning, while Naomi was still at her grandmother's kitchen table finishing toast that had gone cold. Brendan had sent it to the group chat with a single line: this is happening two streets from your grandma's place. The clip showed a flooded intersection, a man clinging to a street sign, brown water pulling a mailbox sideways. Someone behind the camera was shouting in a language Naomi couldn't place. Her grandmother's tap dripped into the sink, and outside the window the street was dry enough to crack.

She watched it three times. The third time she noticed the quality of the light, and after that she couldn't stop noticing it, the way you can't stop feeling a tooth once the dentist names it. It was summer light in the video, hard and high. It was November here. She typed a reply, deleted it, and typed another. Jasmine had already sent three fire emojis and the word SHARE THIS. Naomi put the phone face down on the oilcloth and picked up her grandmother's percolator to refill her cup, and realized she was doing the thing she always did, forwarding first and wondering later, and that she had no idea how to reverse the order.

"I want to check something before I send it," she said. Her grandmother was at the stove, coaxing a second pot of coffee out of grounds that had already given everything they had. "Check it how?" "I don't know yet," Naomi said, and it felt strange and clean to say that out loud.

The following June, she had sat on this same porch with her grandfather while he read the paper, and she remembered him turning a page and pausing over a photograph. "The paper says this was yesterday," he had told her, tapping the caption with one arthritic finger. "But the soldier's coat is wrong for the year they claim." She had been sixteen and had laughed a little, kindly, at how long it took him. Now she wished she had asked what he did next, whether he wrote a letter, whether he simply set the paper down and let the wrongness sit in his lap. He was gone by spring, and the porch chair he used had been left where it was, wicker gone silver.

She took the phone back out. She had heard people talk about reverse image searches, the way you hear about a tool that other, more organized people use. She copied the video's link and pasted it into the search bar, and the engine returned nothing useful, a shrug of blue links about file types and compression. She tried another engine. Nothing. She sat with the sour feeling that the internet had made a promise and quietly withdrawn it, and it would have been easy to give up there, easy to write "not sure, be careful" and let the fire emojis burn on without her.

Then she thought about frames. A video was only pictures in a row, and pictures were what the engines searched. She dragged the little progress bar to the moment the mailbox tipped, paused it, took a screenshot. The frame was blurry with motion, so she moved back a second, paused again, screenshotted again, until she had four stills from the clip saved to her camera roll. She uploaded the clearest one. The results loaded slowly over her grandmother's ancient router, the page rebuilding itself line by line, and then there they were: the same intersection, the same shouting man, dated three summers ago, from a storm in a country an ocean away, embedded in a local news article with a headline in that language she couldn't place.

"Grandma," she said. "Your internet is a crime scene, but it worked." Her grandmother brought two cups over and sat down, and Naomi showed her the video and then the article, side by side. "You can't search a video like this," she said. "You screenshot the frames and search those." Her grandmother squinted at the small screen, held it at arm's length, and nodded the way she nodded at bank statements. "So Brendan is wrong," she said. "Or Brendan was fooled," Naomi said, and felt the difference between those two sentences sit down at the table with them.

She typed to the chat: this is real, but it's from three years ago, not here, link below. Then she added, if you want to check one, this is how I did it, and pasted the screenshots too. There was a long silence, the kind where you can watch the typing dots appear and vanish. She understood, waiting, that she hadn't disabused anyone of anything; she had only caught one clip, one morning, and that the next one would arrive tomorrow, and that she would feel the same visceral pull to share first, the certainty flooding her faster than any argument could follow. Whether she would stop and screenshot again was not a habit yet, only a memory of having done it once. But once was a place to stand. Her grandmother refilled her cup without asking, and Jasmine's reply came through at last: wait, you can do that with any video?

Naomi laughed, and outside the dry street lay quiet under the November sky, and she started typing.

activity: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
story:
The classroom smelled of whiteboard marker and the radiator's burnt dust, and Dominic had decided, on balance, that he was going to be excellent at this. He had read four articles on interviewing the night before, or possibly three, and he had retained all of the important ones, or the important parts of the important ones, which amounted to the same thing. Ms. Visser had arranged the desks into a interviewing setup at the front, one chair behind the other, a legal pad on the desk to make it official. Molly went first. She sat with her shoulders squared and said she was applying at the garden centre because she genuinely valued horticulture, which was a lie, since Dominic had watched her kill a cactus in biology by forgetting it existed. Her answer was fluent anyway. It occurred to him that fluent lying might be a skill, and that he had it too, though he had never needed to test it.

When her turn ended she came back down the aisle and sat beside him and did not gesticulate the way she usually did when telling a story, hands carving the air, but folded them in her lap as though conserving energy for the next round. "He's going to say tell me about yourself," she said. "He meaning Ms. Visser. She said it to Johan, she said it to me. Have yours ready."

Dominic did have his ready. He had rehearsed it in the shower, and in the mirror, and once quietly during chemistry, which Mr. Whatever-his-name-was had generously overlooked. He was, if anything, overprepared, an autodidact of the job interview, self-taught out of necessity since his father's advice had consisted entirely of "don't be weird."

Johan leaned across the aisle, holding a folded printout like evidence. "My grandfather made me practise handshakes at Easter dinner," he said. "Two hours. My arm still hurts. He's obsessed."

"With handshakes," Molly said.

"With one study. He keeps the printout in his wallet." Johan unfolded the page and flattened it on Dominic's desk. "A 2000 study led by a psychologist named William Chaplin found that people with firm handshakes tended to make more favorable first impressions. That's it, that's the whole thing. He's had it in there since before I was born, I think."

"That's the one I read," Dominic said, which was almost true. He had read something about handshakes, and he remembered it involving eye contact and a different decade, but the shape of it was familiar, and the shape of a thing was most of the thing. "Firm handshake, strong eye contact, same principle."

"They're not the same principle," Johan said mildly. "The study's about handshakes."

Dominic waved this off, because the interview was starting, and because he had a system. Ms. Visser called his name. He crossed to the front chair, extended his hand, and held the grip with what he judged to be calibrated firmness, looking directly into her eyes the entire time, which he had read, somewhere, was the actual key, whatever Johan's photocopy said. Ms. Visser shook his hand and made a small note on the legal pad, and he could not read it from that angle, which was probably fine.

"Tell me about yourself," she said.

He told her. He had worked the passage down to ninety seconds, and he delivered it with the steadiness of a boy who had definitely not practised it during chemistry, and she nodded along and made two more notes, and he felt the system working, the machinery of first impressions turning over in his favour, the handshake already forgotten in his favour. He answered a question about weaknesses with a weakness that was secretly a strength, which the articles agreed was the move.

At the end she set down her pen. "Dominic. Look at me for a second." He did. "Your eyes," she said, "were excellent. But you never stopped watching my face, even when I asked about scheduling, which was a bit like being interviewed by a lighthouse. And when I shook your hand, you were so busy maintaining eye contact that you forgot to actually shake it. It was like holding a dead fish that was staring at me."

"It was firm," Dominic said. "I calibrated it."

"It wasn't. And half the time you were looking at my forehead."

He walked back down the aisle. Johan slid the printout toward him without a word, the page turned to the single sentence, and Molly said, "You could take the fish thing as feedback."

Dominic looked at the sentence for a long moment, at the firm handshakes and the favorable first impressions, at the one measurable thing underneath all his reading, and then he turned and called back up the room, "Can we do it again? The handshake part, just that part."
